title: honor, not worship
hook: "isn't praying to Mary idolatry?" — the answer is one difference

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rosary, a string that keeps count. Today, the question a friend may have asked you about Mary.

Sooner or later a friend asks it, usually kindly: why do Catholics pray to Mary? Isn't that worshiping a statue? Walk into an old church and you can see why they'd wonder. Plaster figures in niches. Faces in stained glass. Candles flickering in front of a woman in blue and a man holding keys. Plenty of people raised Catholic were never given the answer either. It turns on one difference, and it's a difference people already live by.
screen: `WHY PRAY TO MARY?` → `A WOMAN IN BLUE. A MAN WITH KEYS.` → `ONE DIFFERENCE.`

segments.voice: Catholics draw a sharp line between worship and honor. Worship belongs to God alone. Honor can be given to people: the way you'd honor a grandmother, a teacher, a hero. Saints get honor. Mary, the mother of Jesus, gets the highest honor of any saint, but still honor, not worship. So why pray to them? Because what Catholics are doing is asking: pray for me. It's what you'd ask a friend. Catholics believe in what the old creed calls the communion of saints: everyone who belongs to Christ, living and dead, is one family, and the family can still pray for each other. Death doesn't end the friendship. So a statue works like a family photo. Nobody is praying to the plaster. And the saints were never perfect. The man with the keys is Peter, who said three times, the night Jesus was arrested, that he didn't know him, then went out and wept. Catholics count him the first pope. A saint isn't someone who never fell. It's someone who kept getting up. Other Christians see it differently: many Protestants honor the saints as examples, and don't ask for their prayers.
screen: `WORSHIP: GOD ALONE.` · `HONOR: MARY AND THE SAINTS.` · `PRAY FOR ME.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of someone, alive or gone, who failed at something and kept going. On the first breath, picture their face. On the second, remember what they got wrong. On the third, remember that they kept going.
The saints. Holy ones: honored, not worshiped, and still one family with the living. Fifth word.
Your line: the company you're in. Flawed people, still going, still in the family. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Mary and the saints, ask for their prayers, and keep their feast days through the year and on All Saints' Day, November 1; worship is given to God alone.

trapdoor: what you thought: Catholics pray to statues.
what it means: worship goes to God alone; the saints are honored, and asked to pray, like friends.
what a scholar hears: latria, worship due to God alone, and dulia, the honor given to saints (hyperdulia for Mary); sanctorum communio, the communion of saints, from the Apostles' Creed.

story.title: the rooster
story.text: Hours before his arrest, Jesus tells Peter he'll deny him three times before the rooster crows. Peter swears he'd die first. That night, warming his hands at a fire in a courtyard, Peter is recognized by a servant girl: you were with him. No, he says. Twice more someone presses him, and the last time he swears he never knew the man. A rooster crows. Peter remembers, goes outside, and weeps bitterly.

wrong.myth: Catholics worship Mary and the saints.
wrong.truth: worship belongs to God alone. Mary and the saints are honored, and asked to pray, the way you'd ask a friend.
